original_interpretation: A 1996 account stated that DRAM prices typically decline 25-30% a year as volumes increase.
evidence_found: "Typically, DRAM prices decline 25 to 30 percent a year as sales volumes increase." (Christian Science Monitor, 'Memory-Chip Prices Rebound a Little Bit After 80 Percent Drop', 4 Oct 1996)
notes: Claim is framed as what the 1996 account said, so reported_claim with a news source is honest. It is a journalist's rule of thumb, not a measured series.

original_interpretation: Micron reported that average selling prices for semiconductor memory fell by over 75% in its fiscal 1996.
evidence_found: "a severe decline (over 75%) in average selling prices for semiconductor memory" (Motley Fool conference-call synopsis, Micron Q4 & FY96; fiscal year ended 29 Aug 1996)
notes: Secondhand: the source is a Motley Fool synopsis of Micron's FY96 results/call, not Micron's own filing; 'news' source_type is appropriate. The 10-K would be the primary source.

original_interpretation: After the 1986 Arrangement, MITI cut Japanese semiconductor output and exports to raise prices, effectively an 'antidumping' voluntary export restraint aimed at a price target.
evidence_found: "To prevent worldwide dumping, MITI did the only thing it knew how to do-reduce the quantity of semiconductors exported to raise export prices. MITI essentially imposed an 'antidumping' voluntary export restraint (VER)-an export restraint designed to meet a price target rather than a quantitative target. MITI issued directives to reduce output but had no statutory authority to force any firm to comply" (Irwin, NBER chapter, p. 11)
notes: Irwin stresses MITI issued directives but lacked authority and had difficulty getting compliance; 'cut output' should be read as MITI directing cuts. claim_type 'estimate' is a poor fit; this is an academic historical account (closer to reported/fact).

original_interpretation: Irwin reports that MITI-induced cutbacks gave Japanese producers a windfall, with profits on 1M DRAM sales of about US$1.2 billion in 1988 alone (historical).
evidence_found: "The MITI-induced production cutbacks generated an enormous windfall for exporters. According to some reports, profits on 1M DRAM sales for Japanese producers amounted to $1.2 billion in 1988 alone" (Irwin, NBER chapter, p. 11, section 1.6)
notes: Irwin cites 'some reports'; the figure is secondhand in the chapter.

original_interpretation: Irwin reports that higher DRAM prices after 1986 hurt computer makers, who formed the Computer Systems Policy Project in 1989 to oppose the antidumping provisions (historical).
evidence_found: "The clear losers from the agreement were semiconductor users, particularly computer manufacturers dependent on DRAMS." (p. 12); "U.S. DRAM prices soared and proved so costly to purchasers ... IBM, Tandem, and Hewlett-Packard led others in founding the Computer Systems Policy Project (CSPP) in 1989 to oppose the antidumping measures." (p. 12, section 1.7)

original_interpretation: Irwin reports that DRAM sales accounted for as much as 60% of Texas Instruments' profits in 1988 and Micron's sales rose sixfold between 1986 and 1988 (historical).
evidence_found: "DRAM sales reportedly accounted for as much as 60 percent of TI'S profits in 1988 and Micron's sales rose by a factor of six between 1986 and 1988." (Irwin, NBER chapter, pp. 11-12)
notes: 'reportedly' in source.

original_interpretation: Hefei government-linked investors owned 36.8% of CXMT at its July 2026 IPO, and state ownership was roughly half including Anhui provincial entities.
evidence_found: "Hefei government-linked investors own 36.8% of CXMT, making them the largest shareholder group." "CXMT's state ownership rises to roughly half after taking into account Anhui provincial government-backed entities' stake." (Reuters analysis republished by BusinessDay, 23 Jul 2026)
notes: Written the day before listing ('scheduled to start trading on the Shanghai Stock Exchange on Monday'), so the stake is pre-/at-listing, as stated. Content is Reuters wire copy; 'news' classification fine. Prospectus would be the primary source.

original_interpretation: CXMT was founded in 2016 by an investment vehicle of Hefei's economic and technology development zone with initial funding of CNY 10 million.
evidence_found: "The company was founded in 2016 by an investment vehicle under the economic and technology development zone of Hefei, the capital city of eastern China's Anhui province, with an initial funding of just 10-million yuan (about $1.5m)." (Reuters via BusinessDay, 23 Jul 2026)

original_interpretation: In early 2023 three state-linked investors including the Big Fund injected CNY 49 billion into YMTC, doubling its registered capital to over CNY 105 billion, after YMTC was added to the US Entity List in December 2022.
evidence_found: "The latest three investors have provided 49 billion yuan (US$7.1 billion), doubling YMTC's registered capital to over 105 billion yuan." Investors named: the Big Fund, Changjiang Industry Investment Group, Hubei Changsheng Development. "YMTC was added to a US export control list in December 2022" (eeNews Europe, 7 Mar 2023)
notes: Source says 'a US export control list' (the Entity List, per other sources). 'Early 2023' inferred from the March 2023 publication date and registry-based reporting; exact registration date not given. Source adds that the Big Fund's direct share was about US$1.9bn (per Bloomberg).

original_interpretation: In late 2023 China's Big Fund invested CNY 14.56 billion (about US$2 billion) in Changxin Xinqiao, a CXMT affiliate building a 12-inch memory wafer base.
evidence_found: TechNode (1 Nov 2023): "China's state-backed 'Big Fund' for chip-making has invested RMB 14.56 billion ($1.99 billion) in domestic memory chip company Changxin Xinqiao"; it "has applied to build a manufacturing base for 12-inch memory wafers." TechNode does not mention CXMT. Asia Financial (31 Oct 2023): "Its general manager is Zhao Lun, who is also the chairman and general manager of Changxin Memory Technology"
correction: Amount and date verified. The cited source (SRC-0384) does not say Changxin Xinqiao is a CXMT affiliate, and says it has 'applied to build' (not is building) the 12-inch base. The affiliate link is supported only indirectly by a shared general manager (Asia Financial, tier 3; new claim in this batch). Stake was 33.15% of registered capital.
notes: Classification fine.

original_interpretation: TrendForce reported in May 2024 that negotiations for 2025 HBM pricing had already begun in 2Q24, with suppliers preliminarily raising prices 5-10%.
evidence_found: "negotiations for 2025 HBM pricing have already commenced in 2Q24. However, due to the limited overall capacity of DRAM, suppliers have preliminarily increased prices by 5–10%" (TrendForce press release, 6 May 2024)

original_interpretation: TrendForce estimated HBM3E TSV yields at only 40-60% in May 2024.
evidence_found: "the yield rates for HBM3e's TSV currently range only from 40% to 60%, with room for improvement" (TrendForce, 6 May 2024)
notes: Point-in-time estimate (May 2024); likely superseded by later yield improvements, so do not use as a current figure.

original_interpretation: TrendForce projected in May 2024 that HBM would exceed 20% of DRAM market value in 2024 and potentially 30% in 2025, while being about 5% of DRAM bit capacity in 2024.
evidence_found: "HBM's share of total DRAM bit capacity is estimated to rise from 2% in 2023 to 5% in 2024 and surpass 10% by 2025. In terms of market value, HBM is projected to account for more than 20% of the total DRAM market value starting in 2024, potentially exceeding 30% by 2025." (TrendForce, 6 May 2024)
notes: Projection, correctly typed as estimate. Actual 2024/2025 shares may since be available from TrendForce; this record should not be read as an outturn.

original_interpretation: TrendForce said in May 2024 that HBM unit prices were several times those of conventional DRAM, about five times DDR5.
evidence_found: "HBM's unit sales price is several times higher than that of conventional DRAM and about five times that of DDR5." (TrendForce, 6 May 2024)
notes: Researcher's paraphrase is accurate; verbatim now supplied. As of May 2024; the 2025-26 conventional DRAM price surge will have changed the ratio.

original_interpretation: SK hynix's head of HBM sales said in February 2024 that its planned 2024 HBM production volume was already sold out.
evidence_found: "Our planned production volume of HBM this year has already sold out" (Kitae Kim, Vice President, Head of HBM Sales & Marketing, SK hynix; eeNews Europe, 27 Feb 2024)
notes: SRC-0386 URL is a WordPress JSON API endpoint for the article, not the article page; content is the eeNews article.

original_interpretation: In March 2024 Micron said its HBM was sold out for calendar 2024 and the overwhelming majority of its 2025 supply was already allocated.
evidence_found: "Our HBM is sold out for calendar 2024, and the overwhelming majority of our 2025 supply has already been allocated." (Sanjay Mehrotra, Micron FQ2 2024 earnings call, 20 Mar 2024; MarketBeat transcript)
notes: Transcript on an aggregator (tier 3); reported_claim is correct.

original_interpretation: Micron said its sold-out HBM contracts are long-term agreements that fix both pricing and volumes along with other stricter terms.
evidence_found: "So some of our discussions with customers, particularly with respect to HBM, when we talk about that HBM is sold out, those types of contracts have both pricing as well as volumes as well as other stricter terms baked in as part of our LTAs." (Micron FQ2 2024 call, 20 Mar 2024)
notes: 'fix' is a slight strengthening of 'have ... baked in'; acceptable.

original_interpretation: Micron said HBM3E consumes about three times the wafer supply of DDR5 to produce the same number of bits on the same technology node.
evidence_found: "Industry-wide, HBM3E consumes approximately three times the wafer supply as D5 to produce a given number of bits in the same technology node." (Micron FQ2 2024 call, 20 Mar 2024)
notes: Micron framed it as an industry-wide ratio, not Micron-specific.

original_interpretation: Samsung's Device Solutions (chip) division posted an operating loss of KRW 2.18 trillion in Q4 2023 on revenue of KRW 21.69 trillion, while its DRAM business returned to profit on higher prices.
evidence_found: "The DS Division posted KRW 21.69 trillion in consolidated revenue and KRW 2.18 trillion in operating losses in the fourth quarter of 2023." "The DRAM business posted a profit on the back of higher prices." (Samsung Q4/FY2023 results release, 31 Jan 2024)
notes: 'returned to profit' implies earlier losses; the release only says it 'posted a profit' (DRAM-level quarterly losses are not disclosed separately). Earnings press release is company_documentation; 'fact' is acceptable for audited-basis reported results.

original_interpretation: Samsung's capital expenditure reached KRW 53.1 trillion in 2023, with memory spending focused on Pyeongtaek infrastructure and HBM/DDR5 capacity despite the downturn.
evidence_found: "The Company's capital expenditures in 2023 reached a total of KRW 53.1 trillion, including KRW 48.4 trillion spent in the Device Solutions (DS) Division and KRW 2.4 trillion in Samsung Display Corporation (SDC)." "Spending on memory was concentrated on building out infrastructure at the facility in Pyeongtaek, Korea and expansion of production capacity of HBM, DDR5 and other advanced nodes." (Samsung Q4/FY2023 release)
notes: 'despite the downturn' is the researcher's framing, not the release's. DS share was KRW 48.4tn.

original_interpretation: Inference: in the 2022-23 downturn every major memory maker responded with output cuts (Kioxia ~30% from Oct 2022, Micron ~20% from Nov 2022, Samsung from April 2023), yet losses were still large (Micron FY2023 GM -9.1%, SK hynix 2023 op loss KRW 7.73tn), and inventory write-downs (Micron ~US$1.83bn) turned price falls directly into losses.
evidence_found: Components verified: CLM-1130 (Kioxia ~30% from Oct 2022), CLM-1124 (Micron ~20%, Nov 2022), CLM-1129 (Samsung 7 Apr 2023 plan to cut production), CLM-1121 (Micron FY23 GM -9.1%), CLM-1126 (SK hynix op loss KRW 7.73tn), CLM-1122 (write-downs ~US$1.83bn). No component claim documents an SK hynix output cut.
correction: Numbers match their verified component claims. 'Every major memory maker' is not supported by the cited claims: no SK hynix production cut is evidenced (only 2024 capex restraint, CLM-1128). Samsung's April 2023 item is an announced plan, not a start date. 'Directly' in the last clause is interpretation.
notes: Inference; source_ids_checked lists component claims, whose sources were checked by other fact-checkers. Component claims reviewed (their own sources were checked by other fact-checkers, not re-opened here): CLM-1130, CLM-1124, CLM-1129, CLM-1121, CLM-1126, CLM-1122.

original_interpretation: Inference: Samsung kept capital spending high through the 2023 downturn (KRW 53.1tn company capex) and announced production cuts only in April 2023, months after Micron and Kioxia, consistent with the largest producer using downturns to hold share.
evidence_found: 2023 capex KRW 53.1tn (SRC-0388); 2022 capex also "KRW 53.1 trillion, including KRW 47.9 trillion for semiconductors" (Samsung Q4/FY2022 release); Samsung cut announcement 7 Apr 2023 (CLM-1129) vs Kioxia 30 Sep 2022 (CLM-1130) and Micron Nov 2022 (CLM-1124).
correction: Factual parts hold: 2023 capex equalled 2022's KRW 53.1tn (flat, semiconductor portion up from 47.9tn to 48.4tn), and Samsung's cut came about 5-6 months after Kioxia and Micron. The motive (using downturns to hold share) is unevidenced interpretation; Samsung did not state it.
notes: Correctly typed as interpretation. Component claims reviewed (their own sources were checked by other fact-checkers, not re-opened here): CLM-1129, CLM-1130, CLM-1124.

original_interpretation: Inference: the 2025-26 memory upturn started with legacy DDR4 end-of-life (mid-2025) and AI server demand, accelerated in 4Q25 (conventional DRAM contract +45-50% QoQ) and peaked in 1Q26 (+93-98% QoQ) before slowing (3Q26 forecast +13-18%).
evidence_found: Components: CLM-1139 (Micron DDR4/LPDDR4 EOL notices, June 2025, verified), CLM-1137 (4Q25 +45-50%, verified), CLM-1135 (1Q26 +93-98%, partially verified: HBM inclusion of revenue unclear, price figure fine), CLM-1136 (2Q26 forecast +58-63%), CLM-1131 (3Q26 forecast +13-18%).
correction: What peaked in 1Q26 is the quarterly rate of increase, not prices: contract prices kept rising in 2Q26 (+58-63% forecast) and 3Q26 (+13-18% forecast). AI server demand as a starting driver is not evidenced by the cited component claims. 2Q26 and 3Q26 figures are forecasts, not outturns.
notes: Numbers match components. Component claims reviewed (their own sources were checked by other fact-checkers, not re-opened here): CLM-1139, CLM-1137, CLM-1135, CLM-1136, CLM-1131.

original_interpretation: Inference: memory contracting is shifting from quarterly (and in the 2025 shortage, monthly) price resets toward 3-5 year take-or-pay agreements with price bands and prepayments, a structural change from the pre-2026 model in which customers avoided long fixed-price contracts.
evidence_found: Components: CLM-1161 (pre-2026 quarterly/annual flexible deals, verified), CLM-1138 (monthly quotes, partially verified), CLM-1157 (customers reluctant to sign long-term fixed-price contracts, verified), CLM-1153 (Micron SCAs take-or-pay with min/max pricing, verified), CLM-1148 (3-5 year terms, verified), CLM-1158 (Samsung LTAs 60-70% of capacity, verified), CLM-1160 (industry LTAs 3-5 years, prepayments, take-or-pay 'in some cases', partially verified; JPMorgan attribution).
correction: Take-or-pay with price bands is documented for Micron's Strategic Customer Agreements; for the industry, the evidence (JPMorgan via Korea Herald) says take-or-pay applies only 'in some cases'. Micron's SCAs cover roughly 20% of DRAM volume over their term. So this describes a direction of change led by Micron, not a completed industry-wide shift.
notes: Evidence field should cite component claim ids. Component claims reviewed (their own sources were checked by other fact-checkers, not re-opened here): CLM-1161, CLM-1138, CLM-1157, CLM-1153, CLM-1148, CLM-1158, CLM-1160.

original_interpretation: Inference: states have repeatedly propped up memory makers in downturns: Korea via state-directed creditor support to Hynix (2001-03), Japan via DBJ equity in Elpida (2009), and China via Big Fund and local-government capital for YMTC and CXMT (2016-2026); only the Chinese entrants have grown, while Qimonda (no rescue agreed) and Elpida (rescued, then bankrupt) exited.
evidence_found: "Struggling German memory-chip company Qimonda announced on Sunday a €325-million rescue package by its parent company Infineon, the Saxon regional government, and a Portuguese state bank." (The Local, 21 Dec 2008); "filed for insolvency protection Friday after talks to secure additional rescue funding collapsed" (The Local, 23 Jan 2009). Hynix, the subject of the 2003 US CVD finding (CLM-1173), is today SK hynix with 2023 revenue of KRW 32.77tn (CLM-1126) and 3Q25 operating profit of KRW 11.38tn (CLM-1143).
correction: Two parts are wrong. (1) Qimonda did get a rescue: a EUR 325m package from Saxony, Infineon and a Portuguese state bank was announced in Dec 2008; it went insolvent in Jan 2009 when talks on further funding failed. (2) 'Only the Chinese entrants have grown' ignores Hynix, the supported Korean firm, which became SK hynix, a top-two DRAM maker. The point that states have repeatedly propped up memory makers holds. A corrected interpretation is added in this batch (supersedes CLM-1209).
notes: Interpretation; the Hynix correction is reasoning from verified claims in the database. Component claims reviewed (their own sources were checked by other fact-checkers, not re-opened here): CLM-1173, CLM-1126, CLM-1143, CLM-1174, CLM-1175.

original_interpretation: TrendForce reported that commodity DRAM contract prices fell 34% and spot prices 52% in 3Q08, while world DRAM revenue fell 2.4% QoQ to US$6.355 billion.
evidence_found: "According to DRAMeXchange survey statistics, commodity DRAM contract price dropped 34% and spot price plunged to 52% in Q308." "The WW Q3 DRAM revenue only slightly decreased 2.4% QoQ to 6.355 billion USD." (TrendForce, 10 Dec 2008)
notes: The source's 'plunged to 52%' is ambiguous (fell by 52% vs fell to 52% of earlier level); the claim's reading (fell 52%) is the likely one but carries that ambiguity. Base period for the 34%/52% is not stated (likely QoQ).

original_interpretation: In 3Q08 Taiwanese DRAM vendors had operating margins of -48% to -70%, and Samsung was the only profitable DRAM vendor (about 4% margin), per TrendForce.
evidence_found: "Financial reports showed that Samsung was the only memory vendor which enjoyed profit in this industry. The DRAM OP margin dropped form 5% in Q2 to 4% in Q3. Taiwanese vendors mostly didn't perform well with the OP margin of -48% to -70%." (TrendForce, 10 Dec 2008)
notes: Source says Taiwanese vendors 'mostly' fell in that range, so not every Taiwanese vendor.

original_interpretation: Qimonda reported an average price decline of 63% for its DRAM products in the nine months to June 2008, after prices fell by more than 80% in calendar 2007.
evidence_found: "an average price decline of 63% for our DRAM products" (nine months ended 30 Jun 2008 vs same period 2007); "In the 2007 calendar year, we have experienced a sharp decline of market prices (for 512Mb DDR2 memories in particular) with prices falling by more than 80%." (Qimonda 6-K)
correction: The 63% figure is verified. The >80% fall in calendar 2007 refers to market prices, especially 512Mb DDR2, not Qimonda's average DRAM price. Corrected claim added (supersedes CLM-1212).

original_interpretation: Qimonda reported a net loss of EUR 1,481 million in the nine months ended 30 June 2008, versus net income of EUR 16 million a year earlier.
evidence_found: "Net loss of €1,481 million in the nine months ended June 30, 2008"; net income of €16 million in the nine months ended June 30, 2007 (Qimonda Form 6-K)

original_interpretation: Micron's DRAM revenue was US$60.908 billion in the nine months to 28 May 2026 versus US$19.594 billion a year earlier (about +211%); NAND revenue was US$17.683 billion versus US$6.251 billion.
evidence_found: Note 14 'Revenue and Customer Contract Liabilities', revenue by technology, nine months ended May 28, 2026 / May 29, 2025: "DRAM: $60,908" / "$19,594"; "NAND: $17,683" / "$6,251" (USD millions) (Micron 10-Q, quarter ended 28 May 2026)
notes: Growth recomputed: 60,908/19,594 = 3.108, i.e. +210.8%. The metric population 'incl. HBM' is consistent with Micron reporting HBM within DRAM. Prior-year period ended 29 May 2025. Micron's FY2026 10-K (year ending early Sept 2026) will add full-year figures but does not supersede these nine-month numbers.
